scenario: AITA for catching my parents disputes on a video conference when I'm working from home? | I am in my early 20s and I have a full time job. I'm living at home right now because, right when cuarantine was starting, I tried to renew my apartment lease and my landlord refused me, saying he was selling the building for condos. So with all the shutdowns, I wasn't able to find a new apartment in time and my parents let me move back in. It's really not ideal and I've actually signed a new apartment lease that starts in a month. I wish it was sooner but housing near me is very competitive. My parents have always had a very disfunctional relationship. But they won't leave each other. No matter how much drama they have, I think they've lived like this too long to consider anything else. I have my work setup in the formal dining room which is rarely used. The room opens to the main entry hallway, and there is no door there. So there's less privacy than I'd prefer. I was hosting a meeting this morning and several of my coworkers were attending. They're all actually good friends of mine outside of work too; close enough friends that I've told them about my tumultuous childhood, my stresses moving back in with my family, etc. So when my parents came in the door in a full blown screaming match, in full view of the camera, I wasn't too shaken. First, unfortunately, that kind of thing has been really normalized for me, it doesn't register as a big deal. Second, it wasn't like the people in the meeting didn't already know my parents were high-tempered. So I just said "Hold on, can you still hear me? Not well? Sorry. Let's just take a coffee break then pick up from there." A couple people got up but my coworker Dan who's a good friend of mine stayed and asked me if I was all good. I said yeah, this shit was normal for all my life, I was just annoyed at the timing but I wasn't scared or some shit. My other co-workers trickled back in. My parents were still going hog wild in the hallway, and I eventually said "hey could yall keep it down, I'm presenting for a meeting." My dad saw that they were on camera first, and got really mad at me. Yelling at me to get the fuck out of his house. I went out to my car and took my laptop and finished the meeting in there. But when I came back in my parents were both over yelling at each other for the moment and they were both furious at me for "filming a private family matter for everyone to see" and shit like that. I said that I wasn't trying to film them, I was on camera myself because I was doing a presentation and they walked right in and started screaming. And if they'd stopped to think or look around at all they'd see I was trying to work quietly. My parents kicked me out and I'm at a hotel now. My parents want an apology and I don't know what to do. I think I might to keep the peace but I don't really feel bad for what I did. AITA for getting my parents argument on a video conference?

The user is in their early 20s, living with parents due to pandemic housing issues, and just had a work meeting where their parents' argument was visible on camera. Now they're being blamed for "filming a private family matter" and kicked out. They're asking if they're the asshole (AITA) for this situation.

First, I need to recall the AITA framework. It's about whether the user's actions were unreasonable or inconsiderate in a social context. The key is whether they violated norms of respect, privacy, or basic courtesy. 

Looking at the scenario: 
- The user has a work setup in a dining room with no door, so it's not a private space. 
- They were hosting a work meeting with colleagues who already know about their family dynamics (they've shared details about their "t tumultuous childhood" and stress of moving back in). 
- When parents started arguing in the hallway, the user didn't intentionally record them—they were on camera for work. 
- They tried to handle it calmly: "Hold on, can you still hear me?... coffee break," then later asked parents to "keep it down" because they're presenting. 
- Dad saw himself on camera and got angry, then both parents accused the user of "filming a private matter" and kicked them out. 

Hmm... the core issue here is about expectation of privacy versus shared living space. The user didn't intentionally record their parents; the meeting was work-related, and the parents walked into a common area (hallway visible from the dining room). 

Important points to consider:
- The dining room has no door, so it's not a "private" space. Parents entering the hallway is natural in a shared home. 
- Colleague's already aware of family dynamics, so no "exposure" of new sensitive info. 
- User didn't actively film or share the footage—they were just on a work call. 
- Parents' reaction seems disproportionate: "filming a private matter" when they themselves barged into the workspace during a work call. 
- Kicking the user out over this is extreme, especially since they're about to move out in a month. 

Wait— the user said "I wasn't trying to film them, I was on camera myself because I was doing a presentation and they walked right in..." That's key. The onus is on the parents to respect the user's work space, not the other way around. 

Also, the "filming" accusation is technically incorrect. The user didn't record them; they were in a video call. The meeting was work-related, not a personal recording. 

Social norms: 
- In shared living spaces, especially with no barriers, it's expected that family members might be visible during work calls. 
- If the parents didn't want to be seen, they should've avoided the area during work hours. 
- The user's response was calm and professional: "hold on, coffee break," then " keep it down, I'm presenting." 
- Parents' anger seems more about their own embarrassment than any real wrongdoing by the user. 

... and the fact that they kicked the user out over this? That's the real issue. The user didn't do anything wrong—they were just in their own workspace. 

So AITA? No. The parents are the ones acting unreasonably here. 

But let me double-check: 
- Did the user intentionally record or share the argument? No. 
- Did they have a right to work in that space? Yes, as a resident. 
- Did the parents have a right to disrupt a work call in a shared area? No—they should've been mindful. 
- Is "filming a private matter" a valid accusation when it was a work call? No, that's a mischaracterization. 

Final verdict: not the asshole. The parents are overreacting. The user's actions were entirely reasonable. 

... though I should note: the user might want to consider future work setups (e.g., using a different room, even temporarily), but that doesn't make them AITA for this incident. The blame lies with the parents for their behavior and overreaction.
